records.quote: Corollary 5.1. Let Y1, Y2 follow (18). If µ1 ≤ µ2, δ1 ≤ δ2, σ1,ii = σ2,ii for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n and σ1,ij ≤ σ2,ij for all 1 ≤ i ≠ j ≤ n, then P(Y1 > a) ≤ P(Y2 > a) holds for all a ∈ Rn. Furthermore, the foregoing inequality is strict if µ1 < µ2, δ1 < δ2, and σ1,ij < σ2,ij for all 1 ≤ i ≠ j ≤ n.
records.compared: Y1 vs Y2 — tail probabilities P(Y > a) for all orthants (extension of Slepian's theorem)

hypotheses.text: µ1 ≤ µ2, δ1 ≤ δ2, σ1,ii = σ2,ii for all 1 ≤ i ≤ n, σ1,ij ≤ σ2,ij for all 1 ≤ i ≠ j ≤ n
hypotheses.formal: componentwise location/skew ordering + equal variances + covariance ordering

conclusion.direction: P(Y1 > a) ≤ P(Y2 > a) for all a ∈ Rn, i.e., Y1 ≤uo Y2; strict under strict inequalities

records.quantifiers: all a ∈ Rn; all 1 ≤ i, j ≤ n
records.ambiguity: uo is the paper's upper-orthant order — outside the plain vocabulary → 'other: uo' (B's label). Direct consequence of Theorems 4.12/4.15.

note: Printed orthant-probability conclusion; labeled 'other: uo' per vocabulary.

records.quote: Example 4.4. We consider the special case of univariate GLSE distribution to illustrate the results in Lemma 4.3. The survival functions of the GHSS distributions under three parameter setting are plotted in Figure 1(a). It is easy to check that the conditions in Lemma 4.3(1) are satisfied, and thus agrees with the usual stochastic ordering among these three distributions displayed in the plot. Moreover, Figure 1(b) provides a counterexample showing that the survival functions of these distributions cross with each other if the scale parameters of the three distributions are not identical.
records.compared: three univariate GHSS distributions; survival-function ordering in Fig 1(a)

hypotheses.text: conditions in Lemma 4.3(1) satisfied in panel (a); scale parameters differ in panel (b)

conclusion.direction: usual stochastic order verified graphically in Fig 1(a); survival curves cross in Fig 1(b) when σ's differ (counterexample)

records.ambiguity: Graphical evidence only (curves plotted, crossing/non-crossing inspected visually).

note: Supporting graphical example plus a crossing counterexample panel; B's 'counterexample' kind is folded into the example record (single printed Example 4.4).

records.quote: Example 4.8. As an illustration for Lemma 4.7, the stop-loss transformations for the univariate GHSS distributions are plotted in Figure 2. It is easy to check that the conditions in Lemma 4.7(1) are satisfied, and consistent with the increasing convex ordering among these three distributions displayed by the stop-loss transformations in Figure 2(a). Figure 2(b) provides a counterexample under the setting (µ1, σ1, δ1) = (0, 1, 0.5) and (µ2, σ2, δ2) = (1, 2, −0.5). It is noticed that the stop-loss transformations intersect with each other when the conditions in Lemma 4.7 are not satisfied.
records.compared: stop-loss transforms E[(Y − t)+] of three GHSS distributions; icx ordering in Fig 2(a)

hypotheses.text: conditions in Lemma 4.7(1) satisfied in (a); violated in (b) under (µ1,σ1,δ1) = (0,1,0.5), (µ2,σ2,δ2) = (1,2,−0.5)

conclusion.direction: stop-loss transforms ordered consistently with icx in Fig 2(a); they intersect (ordering fails) in Fig 2(b) counterexample

records.quantifiers: three GHSS distributions in (a); two in (b); t ≥ 0
